title: Lattice Search — security + production readiness review (Hosted API + roadmap)
summary: Lattice Search walked Redwood through their internal go-live/security approval requirements for adding an LLM inference provider to an enterprise search product (customer data, regulated customers). Key asks: auditability (who did what / when), SSO/SAML + RBAC, data retention and residency clarity, and a concrete “launch checklist” they can attach to their change-management packet. Redwood clarified Hosted API data handling (no prompt storage by default; limited logs), available security controls today (SOC 2, encryption, key mgmt options depending on deployment), and what’s on the near-term roadmap (richer audit logs in Console, admin controls). Discussion also covered production readiness items: retries/timeouts, rate limiting/quotas, streaming disconnect behavior, and model pinning/fallback. Agreed to share Redwood’s security artifacts + draft production launch checklist, and schedule a technical deep dive on audit logs and Private/VPC options.
topics: Audit logs (Console + API) and admin actions
Production launch readiness checklist (timeouts/retries, quotas, model pinning, fallback)
Dedicated vs Private (VPC) options and timelines
questions: Can Redwood provide audit logs for API key creation, quota changes, model config/pinning, and admin overrides?
Do you store prompts or completions by default, and what is the retention period for request metadata/logs?
Is SSO/SAML supported for Console access and can RBAC restrict who can create keys / change quotas?
Can we pin model versions and define a fallback policy for capacity or quality issues?
How does rate limiting work and can we set budgets/alerts before going live?
If streaming disconnects, what’s the recommended client behavior and do SDKs support reconnect?
What regions are available today and can we ensure EU traffic stays in-region?
What’s the path/timeline to VPC / private deployment if Hosted API doesn’t pass security review?
action_items: Ben Carter — Send Lattice Search the Redwood security packet (SOC 2, subprocessor list, DPA template) and confirm current data retention defaults — due 2025-02-21
Marcus Lin — Provide written answers on audit logging coverage today vs roadmap; include event examples and any current Console audit trail capabilities — due 2025-02-24
Brian Murphy — Share production readiness guidance (timeouts/retries, streaming reconnect, 429/backoff) and relevant SDK docs/snippets — due 2025-02-24
Nikhil Sharma — Share a draft “first production launch” checklist outline that maps to internal approvals (keys, RBAC, quotas/budgets, model pinning, fallback, observability) — due 2025-02-26
Daniel Ruiz — Confirm Lattice’s required go-live controls list (SSO, audit logs, retention, residency) and whether Hosted API can be approved with compensating controls — due 2025-02-26
Schedule — Set up a 60-min technical deep dive on audit logs + deployment modes (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC) — target week of 2025-03-03
next_steps: Redwood to send security packet + written responses on audit logs/retention/residency.
Redwood to send draft production launch checklist to align with Lattice’s internal change-control.
Lattice to share their internal control checklist and decision deadline for Hosted vs VPC/Private.
Book follow-up technical deep dive (platform + security) with Lattice’s infra/security stakeholders.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Lattice Search — security + production readiness review (Hosted API + roadmap)
Date: 2025-02-19
Start time: 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Ben Carter (Redwood Inference)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood Inference)
- Brian Murphy (Redwood Inference)
- Nikhil Sharma (Redwood Inference)
- Sarah Kim (Lattice Search)
- Daniel Ruiz (Lattice Search)
- Maya Patel (Lattice Search)
- Tom Becker (Lattice Search)

Auto-generated summary (may be incomplete)
- Customer requested clearer auditability, SSO/RBAC, and a go-live checklist they can use for approvals.
- Redwood reviewed Hosted API security posture, logging/retention defaults, and production readiness best practices.
- Next steps: send security packet, share checklist draft, schedule technical deep dive.

Topics
1) Internal security approval requirements
2) Audit logs + admin actions
3) Data handling, retention, and residency
4) Production readiness checklist: retries/timeouts, quotas/budgets, model pinning/fallback, observability

Action items
- Redwood: send security artifacts and checklist draft; follow up with audit log coverage.
- Lattice: share required controls and timeline for approval.

Transcript

[00:00] Ben Carter: Alright, cool. Folks can hear me okay?

[00:03] Sarah Kim: Yep.

[00:04] Daniel Ruiz: Yeah, you’re good.

[00:06] Ben Carter: Great. Thanks everyone for making time. I’m Ben, I work with our PLG and enterprise motion. I pulled in Marcus from security and Brian from the API side, and Nikhil who owns product for Hosted API. 

[00:18] Ben Carter: My understanding is you’re close to a pilot but you’ve got a security gate plus a… like a production readiness sign-off, and you want to make sure we can meet those before you choose Hosted versus, you know, VPC or private.

[00:31] Maya Patel: Yep, exactly. We can do a small proof, but for anything touching customer content we need to attach a pretty thorough packet to our change request.

[00:41] Sarah Kim: And we’ve been burned by vendors that say “we have SOC2” but then there’s no audit trail of what admins can do, or unclear retention. So we want to be really explicit.

[00:52] Ben Carter: Makes sense. Why don’t we do quick intros and then we’ll walk through your checklist.

[01:00] (Introductions)

[01:02] Sarah Kim: Sarah, security engineering.

[01:05] Daniel Ruiz: Daniel, platform. I’m the one who gets paged when rate limits happen, so I’m gonna ask the annoying questions.

[01:11] Maya Patel: Maya, product for enterprise search. Our customers are… some regulated, healthcare-ish.

[01:18] Tom Becker: Tom, IT. Mostly identity, SSO, access reviews.

[01:23] Marcus Lin: Marcus, security at Redwood.

[01:25] Brian Murphy: Brian, API ergonomics and gateway integrations.

[01:28] Nikhil Sharma: Nikhil, PM for Hosted API.

[01:32] Ben Carter: Cool. Sarah, do you want to start with the top of the list? What’s required to get a “yes” internally.

[01:39] Sarah Kim: Sure. I’m going to be blunt. We need: 
One, data handling statement—do you store prompts and completions, for how long, where. 
Two, access controls—SSO/SAML, role-based permissions. 
Three, audit logs—who created keys, who changed quotas, who changed models, whatever.
And then a production checklist. Like, we literally need a checkbox doc that says we did rate limit testing, we set budgets, we set a fallback model, we have monitoring.

[02:10] Ben Carter: That’s actually super aligned with what we’re shipping in our Console right now, an onboarding checklist plus a first production launch checklist. Nikhil can talk about that later.

[02:20] Daniel Ruiz: For audit logs, I want it not just “you can log in,” but like any admin action. If someone rotates a key or increases quota, that should be auditable.

[02:32] Marcus Lin: Understood. Let me split it into “what we have today” and “what’s on roadmap.” Today, in Hosted API, we have organization-level access controls in Console. We support SSO for enterprise plans—SAML 2.0—plus SCIM for provisioning, and we have RBAC roles like Org Admin, Developer, Billing, Read-only. 

[02:55] Tom Becker: Okay, SAML and SCIM are table stakes. Do you support enforced MFA?

[03:00] Marcus Lin: Yes, for SSO you can enforce at your IdP. We also support TOTP MFA on native accounts, but most customers go through IdP.

[03:09] Sarah Kim: And audit logs?

[03:11] Marcus Lin: Audit logging: we have an audit trail for authentication events and certain Console actions today, but I want to be careful: it’s not yet complete coverage for every single admin action. We are expanding it. For example, API key creation events are tracked. Quota and billing changes—some are tracked, some are still being wired.

[03:33] Daniel Ruiz: That’s the part I need to pin down. If it’s partial, we might need compensating controls. Like only one admin account, restricted, change management. But I need to know what’s missing.

[03:44] Marcus Lin: Yep. I can send a matrix: action -> audited yes/no -> where you can access it (Console export, API). We also have internal eventing. (There may be a couple things that are “available by request” while we finish UI.)

[04:02] Maya Patel: We’d prefer not “available by request” for production.

[04:05] Ben Carter: Totally fair.

[04:07] Nikhil Sharma: Just to connect the dots, one reason this is top-of-mind is we’re rolling out a checklist in Console that makes these steps explicit for production—API key creation, quotas, budgets, model pinning, fallback policy, observability hooks. That’s not a substitute for audit logs, but it makes it easier to get to a consistent posture.

[04:28] Sarah Kim: Okay, good. Let’s talk data handling. Do you store prompts? Because we have customer content. Some of it is PII.

[04:36] Marcus Lin: Default: we don’t store prompts and completions for training, and we don’t retain request bodies as a general policy. Operational logs contain metadata—timestamps, request IDs, token counts, status codes, latency, and limited error context. If a customer enables debugging or extended logging, that can change. But default is minimal.

[04:58] Daniel Ruiz: “Limited error context” is vague. Does it ever include the prompt?

[05:02] Marcus Lin: By default, no. We work hard to avoid PII in logs. There are edge cases where an upstream error could include a snippet if a client sends it in a header or something—rare, and we sanitize. We can share our telemetry data classification doc.

[05:21] Sarah Kim: Retention period for those operational logs?

[05:24] Marcus Lin: For Hosted API, standard retention for operational metadata is 30 days. Some customers purchase extended retention for audit and analytics. For security logs, we can retain longer depending on plan and region constraints. 

[05:40] Maya Patel: Data residency—can we keep EU requests in EU?

[05:45] Marcus Lin: Yes, we have regional endpoints. If you route to EU region, processing occurs in EU. Control plane metadata—org info—depends on the specific deployment model; for Private/VPC it’s customer-managed networking and you can keep more inside your boundary. We can detail what’s stored where.

[06:06] Daniel Ruiz: We’ve had issues with vendors saying “EU region” but then logs go to the US.

[06:10] Marcus Lin: Right. For us, telemetry and logs are region-scoped; we don’t ship raw request payloads across regions. Some aggregated metrics may be centralized without identifiers. Again, we can document it.

[06:26] Ben Carter: Sarah, do you have a required doc list? Like SOC2, ISO, pen test, etc.

[06:32] Sarah Kim: We need SOC 2 Type II, subprocessor list, DPA, and a security questionnaire. Also, we need an answer on whether you support customer-managed keys.

[06:43] Marcus Lin: For Hosted API, encryption at rest is standard, and we support key management integrations in higher tiers; customer-managed keys are more typical in Dedicated/Private. If CMK is a hard requirement, we should talk about Dedicated or Private.

[06:58] Maya Patel: For now Hosted is easier. But if it can’t pass review, we need a VPC option.

[07:05] Nikhil Sharma: Dedicated gives you isolated capacity but still Redwood-managed control plane. Private is the strongest boundary—VPC or on-prem style. Dedicated/Private have longer lead times.

[07:17] Daniel Ruiz: Okay. Shifting to production readiness. We got bitten by 429s with another provider. What are the knobs here?

[07:26] Brian Murphy: So quotas and rate limits—there are per-org and per-key limits. You’ll see them in Console. For production, we recommend: set explicit limits, add budgets/alerts, and implement retries with exponential backoff for 429 and certain 5xx. In our SDKs we’re adding “production safe defaults” presets—timeouts, retries, idempotency keys where applicable.

[07:51] Daniel Ruiz: Do you have idempotency on generation endpoints?

[07:54] Brian Murphy: For non-streaming requests, yes, we support idempotency keys. Streaming is trickier because you might get partial tokens; we recommend a reconnect strategy that’s “resume by re-request with the same context” rather than strict token resume. Some SDKs now include helpers.

[08:14] Maya Patel: This is where the launch checklist would help. Because internally, we need to prove we did backoff and we tested streaming.

[08:22] Ben Carter: Exactly. We can share the template. It’s basically “First successful call” and “First production launch.” It includes: create key, set env vars, first request, streaming, retries/timeouts, view usage dashboard, set quotas/budgets, pin model, define fallback policy, add observability hooks.

[08:44] Sarah Kim: I like that. But I also want the ability to show auditors “who approved changes.” Do you have approval workflows?

[08:52] Marcus Lin: We don’t have a built-in approval workflow yet like “two-person rule.” What many enterprise customers do is restrict admin privileges and integrate with your internal change process. We can provide audit events to support that. Approval workflows are on our longer-term roadmap.

[09:10] Tom Becker: RBAC granularity—can we separate “can view usage” from “can create keys” from “can change quotas”?

[09:18] Marcus Lin: Today: yes for major categories (billing vs admin vs developer vs read-only). Fine-grained permissions are limited. We can discuss custom roles but it’s not self-serve.

[09:32] Daniel Ruiz: Another big one: model pinning. If you change models under us, we need to know.

[09:38] Nikhil Sharma: We support pinning model versions. You can specify exact model ID or version. We also support fallback policies—if your pinned model is temporarily constrained, you can choose an allowed fallback set, or you can opt out and fail closed.

[09:58] Maya Patel: For enterprise, we probably fail closed, but for internal we might fail open. 

[10:03] Daniel Ruiz: Does fallback happen automatically, like without us knowing?

[10:07] Nikhil Sharma: It’s policy-driven. If you enable it, it can route to a compatible model variant. We log those routing decisions in request metadata. We can also emit events for “fallback occurred.”

[10:20] Sarah Kim: That eventing—can we export it? Like to Splunk.

[10:24] Brian Murphy: Yes, we integrate via webhooks and we have log export options depending on plan. For Private, it’s easier because it’s inside your network.

[10:36] Daniel Ruiz: I’m going to ask the annoying question. If your usage dashboard lags, how do we know we’re not exceeding budgets.

[10:43] Brian Murphy: Usage dashboards are near-real-time but there can be a delay of a few minutes. For hard limits, quotas enforce at the gateway in real time. Budget alerts are based on metered usage; those can lag slightly but are designed for “warn before you hit it.”

[11:03] Daniel Ruiz: Okay. We’ll want hard quotas, not just alerts.

[11:07] Nikhil Sharma: Yep, the checklist explicitly calls out setting quotas for production.

[11:12] Sarah Kim: Circling back to audit logs: do you log things like “quota changed from X to Y” and by whom?

[11:20] Marcus Lin: Some of that exists. I don’t want to overpromise. We can currently capture: actor, action type, timestamp, target resource. The “before/after” fields are being rolled out for certain settings. We can share what’s available now.

[11:42] Maya Patel: If it’s missing, we’ll get blocked. Our auditors ask for before/after.

[11:47] Marcus Lin: Understood. For the near term, we can provide an export via API for the audit events we have. For settings diffs, we may be able to include it for quota and API keys soon. Let me follow up with the exact dates.

[12:05] Ben Carter: And if Hosted doesn’t pass, then the option is Dedicated or Private. Private gives you the ability to keep audit logs and config inside your environment. But it’s a bigger lift.

[12:17] Daniel Ruiz: What’s the realistic timeline for Private? 

[12:20] Ben Carter: Typically 6–10 weeks depending on environment and security review. Dedicated can be faster.

[12:28] Sarah Kim: That might be too slow for us. So we need to see if Hosted can pass with compensating controls.

[12:35] Ben Carter: Yep.

[12:37] (Crosstalk)

[12:38] Maya Patel: Another thing—do you have a “launch checklist” that we can literally attach? Like a PDF?

[12:44] Nikhil Sharma: We can share a doc version, and soon it will be in Console as a checklist UI. It’s not a PDF per se, but we can export the steps.

[12:55] Sarah Kim: I want it to map to controls. Like: “Access control configured” -> “SSO enabled, admin roles limited.” “Logging enabled” -> “audit logs configured.” Etc.

[13:08] Nikhil Sharma: That makes sense. We’ve been designing it as developer-friendly, but we can create an enterprise mapping.

[13:16] Brian Murphy: And from the production side, it includes the bits that reduce support tickets: 401/403 troubleshooting, streaming disconnect guidance, and rate-limit handling. We’ve seen those be the top issues.

[13:32] Daniel Ruiz: Streaming disconnects—what’s the main failure mode? Is it server closing? Client network?

[13:38] Brian Murphy: Usually it’s client or intermediary timeouts—load balancers, proxies. SSE streams can get cut. We recommend keep-alives and reconnect logic. We also recommend setting explicit timeouts. Some SDKs are adding helpers. 

[13:56] Daniel Ruiz: We use Go and Typescript mostly.

[13:59] Brian Murphy: Good, both have work in progress. I can send the latest snippets.

[14:04] Sarah Kim: Can we disable streaming entirely?

[14:06] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, it’s optional.

[14:09] Maya Patel: Observability hooks—do you support tracing? Like OpenTelemetry.

[14:14] Brian Murphy: We support request IDs and you can propagate correlation IDs. For deeper tracing, we have integrations and guidance. A lot of customers log: model, latency, tokens, status, and request ID. We can also send metrics.

[14:30] Daniel Ruiz: Do you have SLOs? Like uptime.

[14:33] Ben Carter: Hosted has published uptime targets; enterprise contracts can include SLAs. Dedicated has stronger guarantees.

[14:41] Sarah Kim: Okay, I’m going to list the blockers for Hosted approval: audit logs with before/after for config changes, and clear statement on retention/residency. If you can give those, we might be good.

[14:56] Marcus Lin: Got it.

[14:58] Ben Carter: And we’ll get you the security packet. 

[15:01] (Short pause)

[15:03] Ben Carter: Do you have a timeline? When do you need to decide.

[15:07] Maya Patel: Two to three weeks. We want to ship a beta to a subset.

[15:12] Daniel Ruiz: The platform changes need to start sooner, so the checklist helps. If we can standardize “what is production ready,” we can move.

[15:21] Nikhil Sharma: That’s exactly why we’re building it. We’ve seen people get stuck on like, first success then surprised by 429s in production.

[15:31] Sarah Kim: One more: do you have a way to prove “no training on our data” contractually.

[15:36] Ben Carter: Yes, that’s part of the DPA and MSA language. We can send the standard clause.

[15:43] Marcus Lin: And we can share our subprocessor list.

[15:47] Tom Becker: For access reviews, can we pull a list of users with roles via API?

[15:52] Marcus Lin: With SCIM you can manage it centrally. For export, we have admin APIs for org membership. I’ll confirm.

[16:03] Daniel Ruiz: Okay. On model changes, if you deprecate a model version, how much notice.

[16:08] Nikhil Sharma: We publish deprecation notices. For pinned versions, we provide a migration window. You can run A/B tests or canaries via your app; in Console we support rollouts for some customers.

[16:24] Maya Patel: That’s good.

[16:26] Sarah Kim: Any known limitations around audit log export?

[16:30] Marcus Lin: Today the export is not as self-serve as we’d like. You can access some events in Console; for raw export we may need to enable it. Again, I’ll be specific in the follow-up.

[16:44] Ben Carter: I think the best next step is: we send you a written response doc that maps your questions, plus the checklist template. Then we schedule a deeper technical session focused purely on audit logs, retention, and deployment modes.

[16:58] Daniel Ruiz: Yeah, and include “what’s required for Private.” If we do that, we need to scope it.

[17:04] Ben Carter: Cool.

[17:06] (Transcription jumps forward; minor gaps)

[21:18] Maya Patel: Sorry, can I ask about budgets. Is it like “spend cap” or just alerts.

[21:23] Brian Murphy: Both. There’s quota enforcement which is a hard cap on throughput or tokens over a period, and there’s budget alerts which are spend-based. Spend-based alerts can’t be perfectly real-time because metering is aggregated, but it’s close.

[21:41] Daniel Ruiz: For the beta we want hard caps.

[21:44] Brian Murphy: Yep. We usually recommend starting conservative.

[22:01] Sarah Kim: And for your new checklist UI, does it show completion per org.

[22:06] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, it tracks progress, and Support can see it too. There will also be admin overrides for troubleshooting. 

[22:14] Sarah Kim: Admin override sounds scary.

[22:16] Nikhil Sharma: It’s permissioned and audited. It’s mostly for support cases where an event didn’t register.

[22:23] Marcus Lin: And we’re careful about PII in those events.

[22:29] Daniel Ruiz: Events—are they emitted client-side or server-side.

[22:33] Brian Murphy: Mostly server-side from the gateway, to avoid spoofing and reduce client complexity. Some hints come from SDK user agent tagging.

[22:45] Sarah Kim: That actually helps. Server-side is more trustworthy.

[23:10] (Discussion on internal approvals)

[28:42] Sarah Kim: Okay, so deliverables from you: security packet, audit log matrix, and the launch checklist.

[28:49] Ben Carter: Yep.

[28:51] Daniel Ruiz: And from us, we’ll send our control checklist and identify what we can accept as compensating controls.

[29:00] Ben Carter: Great.

[29:03] (More Q&A; some crosstalk)

[36:15] Maya Patel: Can you just clarify: if we call the Hosted API, is any of our content used to improve models.

[36:21] Ben Carter: No, not used for training. That’s contractual.

[36:26] Marcus Lin: And operationally we’re not storing prompts by default.

[36:31] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[41:02] Daniel Ruiz: Last one from me: if we get a 500, do you recommend retry.

[41:06] Brian Murphy: Depends on the code. For transient 5xx, yes with jittered backoff. For 4xx, no. For streaming, handle disconnect and retry if you didn’t complete. We can share recommended patterns.

[41:25] Daniel Ruiz: Great.

[46:40] Ben Carter: Alright, I’m going to recap next steps so we’re aligned.

[46:44] Ben Carter: One, we’ll email the security packet—SOC2, DPA template, subprocessors—by end of week. Two, Marcus will send a specific audit log coverage doc, including gaps and near-term timeline. Three, Nikhil will send a draft “first production launch checklist” that maps to the controls you mentioned. Four, Brian will send the production defaults guidance for SDKs, especially around retries/timeouts and streaming.

[47:15] Ben Carter: And then, Daniel, you’ll send us your internal checklist and any hard deadlines.

[47:20] Daniel Ruiz: Yep.

[47:22] Sarah Kim: Works.

[47:24] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone.

[47:27] Ben Carter: Thanks all. We’ll get the follow-up out. 

(End)
